title: Wave of Hoax Bomb Threats Disrupts European Aviation for Second Time This Week
snippet: At least 18 flights across Europe faced emergency diversions, military escorts, and security sweeps following a coordinated series of bomb threats.
content:
European aviation authorities were thrown into high alert Thursday after at least 18 flights across the continent were targeted by bomb threats—marking the second major wave of mid-air security scares in less than a week.

The threats impacted commercial flights across multiple countries, including France, Italy, Spain, Poland, and Austria. While law enforcement officials confirmed that no explosives have been found on any searched aircraft so far, the warnings prompted emergency diversions, runway groundings, and military jet escorts.

Chilling Emails and Fighter Escorts

Among the most severe disruptions was an Aer Lingus flight traveling from Dublin to Rome, which was forced to execute an emergency diversion to Évreux military air base in northern France. In Italy, Air Force fighter jets were scrambled to escort a Finnair flight from Helsinki into Rome’s Fiumicino Airport.

Italian airport authorities revealed that the threats targeting Rome-bound flights arrived via email, signed by a group or individual identifying as "Fighters of the Male State." The messages claimed to target a "feminist regime" and threatened to "turn the skies red" with explosions.

U.K. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander sharply condemned the incidents, characterizing them as "malicious hoax threats."

A Growing Strain on Airline Security

Thursday's wave follows a similar incident just two days earlier, when eight flights—including two originating from the U.K.—were targeted by unconfirmed bomb scares. On Monday, a Wizz Air flight bound for Sofia was escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet following a mid-flight warning.

Aviation security experts emphasize that while false alarms are common in the industry, the sheer volume of synchronized threats over a short window is unusual and concerning.

"If you issue enough hoax threats, then complacency could set in and a real threat could be ignored—or they could be a diversion," warned Philip Baum, a professor of aviation security at Coventry University. Other experts suggested the attacks could be part of a coordinated effort designed to inflict low-cost, deniable disruption on European infrastructure.

International law enforcement agencies are actively investigating the source of the emails, while airlines work to clear grounded aircraft and re-accommodate stranded passengers.
